title: Ananda weeps
hookLine: Ananda weeps outside; the Buddha praises him as the kindest attendant

cards: Hospitals have a particular hallway. The one just outside the room, where family members go to fall apart for a minute so they can walk back in steady.
Ananda has served the Buddha for many years: fetching water, guarding the door, keeping the teachings in memory. Now, at Kusinara, he goes into a dwelling, leans against the door frame, and weeps.
I'm still a learner, he says. I still have work to do. And my teacher, who was so kind to me, is about to pass away.
The Buddha notices he's gone and asks the monks: where is Ananda?

teach.h: DON'T GRIEVE: ALL THAT'S DEAR CHANGES.
teach.b: He sends a monk: go and tell Ananda the teacher is calling him. Ananda comes back, bows, and sits to one side. The Buddha doesn't scold him.
He says: enough, Ananda. Don't grieve, don't lament. Haven't I told you that we must be parted from everything dear to us?
How could anything born, put together, bound to fall apart, not fall apart? Then he thanks him.

teach.h: KINDNESS IN BODY, SPEECH AND MIND.
teach.b: For a long time, Ananda, you've attended on me with kindness in body, in speech and in mind, helpfully, gladly, wholeheartedly, without measure.
You've done well. Keep at it, and you'll soon be free. Then he speaks to all the monks in praise of Ananda.
The Buddhas of the past had attendants as good as Ananda, he says, and so will those of the future.

Ananda is wise. He knows the right time for monks, nuns, lay followers, kings and teachers of other schools to come and see me. And he names something wonderful about him, true for monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen alike.
When any of them come to see Ananda, they're glad just to see him. When he speaks, they're glad to hear him. And when he stops, they wish he'd go on.

Later tradition says Ananda reached awakening the night before the first great council, where he recited the discourses. That, tradition says, is the voice behind their opening words: thus have I heard.

how: Buddhists across traditions honor Ananda as the disciple who remembered and recited the discourses, and the phrase 'thus have I heard' that opens many suttas is traditionally understood as his voice.

o: the attendant's shame at failing his teacher
the mourning song the monks sang at Kusinara
the attendant's grief, met with comfort and praise

p: the Buddha noticing he was gone
the ways Ananda served with kindness
the opening tradition gives to Ananda

s: the Buddha scolds Ananda for weeping
he comforts him, reminds him all that's dear changes, and praises him.
the Buddha says past Buddhas also had attendants as good as Ananda
and so will Buddhas of the future.
Ananda was already fully awakened when he wept
he says he is still a learner; tradition places his awakening before the first council.

games.q: you're the Buddha, near the end. your attendant has slipped out to cry. what do you do?
o: send for him, comfort him, and praise his service in front of everyone.
tell the others not to grieve like him.
games.why: he calls Ananda back, comforts him, thanks him, and praises him to all the monks.

practice: Think of someone who has helped you faithfully, a parent, a nurse, a colleague, a friend who drives you to the airport, and let three things come up: something kind they did, something kind they said, something kind they must have wished for you.
Stay with each for a few breaths. Then let the Buddha's line form for them, quietly: you've done well.

wordCard.voice: Ananda weeps. At Kusinara the attendant cries in a doorway; the Buddha calls him back, comforts him, and praises his years of kindness. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Ananda: joy, delight. the name of the attendant who wept.

carryVoice: Your line: you've done well, Ananda. Near the end, the Buddha made sure everyone in the room knew how good he had been. Day five hundred fifty, done.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), Ananda weeps and is praised
